section_summary: This section covers internal political instability, militarism, and diplomatic developments in Japan from mid-1932 to early 1933, centering on the aftermath of the May 15 Incident and the impending recognition of Manchukuo. U.S. diplomatic reporting from Tokyo, Peiping, and Mexico examines the breakdown of military and academic discipline, unauthorized actions by junior military officers, the provocative role of Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori, and the reorganization of Japanese administration in Manchuria. The materials also trace the completion of the Lytton Commission's report, international reactions to speeches by Premier Saito and Foreign Minister Uchida, and debates within the U.S. State Department over proposing a Pacific conference or maintaining non-recognition.

subfiles.about: Press clipping providing editorial commentary on Sino-Japanese relations, Soviet overtures, and international conference proposals concerning Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Editorial fragment on Manchuria/Shanghai links notes Araki's uncompromising Osaka remarks and Doihara's ten-year Manchukuo timeline, suggesting eventual international-conference admission.
subfiles.title: Press Clipping on Manchurian Issue and Proposed International Conference

subfiles.about: Editorial discussing Prime Minister Saito's responses to Reuter regarding Japan's intentions in Manchuria and maintenance of the Open Door.
subfiles.from: Peking & Tientsin Times
subfiles.summary: Editorial evaluates Saito's Reuter statement on Manchuria policy: Open Door adherence, no annexation or customs union, respecting Russian Chinese Eastern Railway rights, seen as easing Soviet war fears under his cabinet.
subfiles.title: A New Japanese Gesture

subfiles.about: Editorial analyzing Prime Minister Saito's address to the Diet and his policy toward Manchuria, Shanghai, and the League of Nations.
subfiles.from: A. N., Le Journal de Pekin
subfiles.summary: Commentary critiques Saito's Diet speech for ignoring unemployment while pursuing military ambitions, mocking Manchukuo's creation under Pu Yi and a Shanghai Free City proposal, calling the cabinet a militarist front.
subfiles.title: Premier Saito's Speech

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 19 regarding economic relief for Japanese farmers.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grew's Despatch No. 19 on Japanese farmer-relief proposals, filed at 894.61/16.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/422 (Relief of Farmers)

subfiles.about: Cover memorandum submitting Laurence E. Salisbury's summary of Despatch No. 33 to the Secretary of State.
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Hamilton submits Salisbury's summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 33 on Japan's declining discipline to Stimson, endorsed by Hornbeck.
subfiles.title: Submission of Summary of Despatch No. 33 to Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum summarizing Tokyo Despatch No. 33 on the deterioration of discipline in Japan.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes Grew's report on military/student insubordination, citing radical ideas, family-system decay, postwar affluence, and corruption, warning reactionary officers controlled the Manchurian campaign while Japan lacked leadership against isolation.
subfiles.title: Summary of Tokyo Despatch No. 33: Decline of Discipline in Japan

subfiles.about: Comprehensive diplomatic despatch analyzing the causes and manifestations of the breakdown of discipline in Japanese military, academic, and political life.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew details the alarming erosion of discipline in Japan, highlighted by the October 1931 coup plot, the assassination of Premier Inukai on May 15, 1932, and student strikes and university corruption. He examines root causes, such as the disintegration of traditional feudal and patriarchal family bonds, commercial corruption among political parties, and ideological radicalism. Grew warns that an undisciplined clique of junior military officers now dominates policy in Manchuria and Tokyo, threatening national solvency and risking grave international isolation.
subfiles.title: Decline of Discipline in Japan (Despatch No. 33)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing a report from Tokyo on widespread public discontent and the danger of further political assassinations.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury highlights Despatch No. 35: a Tokyo police official warned the attaché Japan is full of malcontents, young officers are uncontrollable, and more assassinations are likely.
subfiles.title: Summary of Despatch No. 35: Unrest in Japan

subfiles.about: Confidential despatch reporting frank observations on political unrest and danger of assassinations made by a Tokyo police officer to the Military Attaché.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew relays a Tokyo police official's candid warning to the Military Attaché of pervasive discontent, uncontrolled young officers, self-serving politicians like Adachi, anger over nepotism, and likely further assassinations.
subfiles.title: Unrest in Japan (Despatch No. 35)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing a memorandum by Secretary of State Stimson regarding reports of military control in Tokyo.
subfiles.from: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Stimson's memo on reports that Japan's government is virtually controlled by younger Army officers.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/425 (Secretary Stimson Memorandum)

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 43 enclosing an open letter from the Shiunso to the League Commission of Inquiry.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's Despatch No. 43, enclosing Shiunso's open letter to the League Commission, led by Tetsuma Hashimoto.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/426 (Despatch No. 43)

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting an open letter addressed to the Lytton Commission by the reactionary nationalist society Shiunso.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew transmits the Shiunso's open letter opposing political parties, linking the chauvinist group (led by Hashimoto) to Finance Minister Inoue's earlier assassination and explaining its uncompromising Manchuria stance.
subfiles.title: Open Letter from a Reactionary Society to the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry (Despatch No. 43)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Open letter published by the nationalist Shiunso organization demanding that the League of Nations recognize Japan's vital position in Manchuria.
subfiles.from: The Shiunso, Tokyo
subfiles.summary: The Shiunso issues a militant manifesto to the League Commission of Inquiry asserting that Japan will never retreat an inch from its acquired rights in Manchuria and Mongolia, which constitute Japan's national life line. The letter justifies the establishment and prompt recognition of Manchukuo by citing historical autonomy, the Nine-Power Treaty, and the U.S. recognition of Panama in 1903. It condemns traditional Chinese diplomacy, attacks American support of Chinese anti-Japanese boycotts, and sets forth seven specific demands for the Commission's report.
subfiles.title: An Open Letter to the Members of the League of Nations Commission of Inquiry
subfiles.to: League of Nations Commission of Inquiry

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Kenzo Adachi's plans to form the Kokumin Domei and urging immediate recognition of Manchukuo.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Minister to China
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays Adachi's plan to form the Kokumin Domei; Adachi and War Minister Araki agreed the time was ripe for Manchukuo recognition, possibly preceding the League meeting given Lytton Report and Stimson-speech resentment.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 942 from Peiping (Adachi and Manchukuo Recognition)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum analyzing Despatch No. 69 regarding the indiscipline and political influence of Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury reviews Grew's report on Foreign Office spokesman Shiratori's unauthorized, contradicting statements, explaining he's protected by military-fascist and Hiranuma ties, and that his leaks damage frank diplomatic relations.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Despatch No. 69: The Foreign Office Spokesman

subfiles.about: Despatch examining the controversial career, political affiliations, and disruptive press statements of Foreign Office spokesman Toshio Shiratori.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew provides a biographical sketch of Toshio Shiratori, Director of the Foreign Office Bureau of Information and Intelligence, explaining how he exemplifies Japanese dual diplomacy. Despite past attempts by Foreign Ministers Shidehara and Yoshizawa to dismiss him, Shiratori maintains his post due to familial prestige and close ties to Baron Hiranuma and the militarist Kokuhonsha. Grew observes that Shiratori's habit of leaking and distorting confidential diplomatic conversations to reporters greatly complicates embassy business.
subfiles.title: The Foreign Office Spokesman (Despatch No. 69)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Cross-reference sheet indexing Tokyo Despatch No. 72 on the merger of two major Japanese proletarian parties.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to Grew's Despatch No. 72 on the amalgamation of Japan's two largest proletarian parties, filed at 894.504/40.
subfiles.title: Document File Note: 894.00/429 (Amalgamation of Proletarian Parties)

subfiles.about: Despatch reporting on the formation of the Social Masses Party (Shakai Taishuto) through the merger of Japanese proletarian factions.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Ambassador Grew reports on the merger of Japan's two leading proletarian political groups into the Shakai Taishuto (Social Masses Party) to overcome factional weakness. The despatch translates the party's manifesto and comprehensive platform, which seeks to protect workers and peasants, dismantle capitalism, and overthrow the nobility. Key planks include state-financed education, public medical care, agricultural debt relief, agrarian credit banks, reduction of armaments, and abolition of capitalistic imperialism.
subfiles.title: Amalgamation of Proletarian Parties (Despatch No. 72)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Telegram reporting Chinese official press reactions to Foreign Minister Uchida's speech and denying rumors regarding a naval base on Hainan Island.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Minister to China
subfiles.summary: Johnson relays a Chinese editorial saying Uchida's Diet speech preempts international action before Manchukuo recognition, lamenting Japan's treaty violations; also transmits China's denial that Hainan was being leased as a U.S. naval base.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1023 from Peiping (Uchida Diet Speech and Hainan Denial)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Internal charge slip recording the temporary routing of document 894.00/430.
subfiles.from: Department of State
subfiles.summary: Standard charge slip records checkout and routing of file 894.00/430, with clerical tracking notations.
subfiles.title: Charge Slip for File 894.00/430

subfiles.about: Personal and strictly confidential letter evaluating political developments in Tokyo, the timing of Manchukuo's recognition, and Foreign Office personalities.
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, U.S. Ambassador to Japan
subfiles.summary: Grew privately tells Stimson that Manchukuo recognition might wait for the League's Lytton Report action unless army radicals force it sooner, noting Saito's consolidating power and calling spokesman Shiratori Tokyo's enfant terrible.
subfiles.title: Personal Letter from Ambassador Grew to Secretary Stimson
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Memorandum summarizing a report from Mexico City regarding a frank conversation with Japanese Minister Yoshiatsu Hori.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury summarizes a Mexico City conversation: Minister Hori called the military dominant in Japan, warned of spreading campus communism, and doubted Manchuria's practical benefits.
subfiles.title: Summary of Mexico Despatch No. 1797: Conversation with Japanese Minister

subfiles.about: Diplomatic despatch transmitting a memorandum of conversation with the Japanese Minister to Mexico concerning internal Japanese affairs.
subfiles.from: J. Reuben Clark, Jr., U.S. Ambassador to Mexico
subfiles.summary: Clark transmits a confidential memo of his August 1932 dinner talk with Japanese Minister Hori on Japan's political and economic instability.
subfiles.title: Political and Economic Conditions in Japan (Despatch No. 1797)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: Memorandum recording Japanese Minister Hori's candid assessments of military dominance, economic depression, communism, and Soviet fishery disputes.
subfiles.from: J. Reuben Clark, Jr., U.S. Ambassador to Mexico
subfiles.summary: Clark records Hori's dinner remarks lamenting unchecked military dominance, scarce wise civilian leadership, and rising campus communism; economically, falling rice prices, depressed silk exports, doubtful Manchurian migration value, and friction-laden Soviet salmon fisheries.
subfiles.title: Memorandum of Conversation between Ambassador Clark and Japanese Minister Hori

subfiles.about: State Department summary and digest of an article from The Round Table analyzing the Far Eastern crisis, British policy, and international treaties.
subfiles.from: Eugene H. Dooman, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Dooman digests a Round Table article on British China policy, Washington Conference interdependence, and Japan's economic population pressures, arguing Manchurian intervention can't solve its economy and framing non-recognition as a League/Kellogg Pact test.
subfiles.title: Digest of Article 'The Far East' in The Round Table

subfiles.about: Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum analyzing Minister Johnson's proposal for an international conference on the Far East.
subfiles.from: Wallace R. Little, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Wallace R. Little analyzes Minister Johnson's recommendation that the United States sponsor an international conference in Geneva or Tokyo to address Far Eastern issues. Little argues that a new conference is premature because Japan's military leaders are fully committed to exploiting Manchuria and will not yield except to superior force. He contends that prolonged Chinese guerrilla resistance, financial strain, and firm Western non-recognition will eventually force Japan to reconsider its policy, much like earlier failed interventions in Siberia.
subfiles.title: Reactions to Minister Johnson's Telegram of September 7, 1932

subfiles.about: Confidential telegram reporting the completion and dispatch of the Lytton Report and proposing an international conference to resolve Pacific tensions.
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, U.S. Minister to China
subfiles.summary: Minister Johnson reports that the Lytton Commission signed its report in Peiping on September 4, 1932, and that its commissioners have departed for Europe. Expecting the report to condemn Japanese aggression and anticipating that Japan will sign a treaty guaranteeing Manchukuo around September 15, Johnson warns of Japan's militarist withdrawal from the West. He urges the United States to seize the diplomatic initiative by proposing an international conference, possibly held in Tokyo with Soviet and Chinese participation, to link Far Eastern security with armament limitation.
subfiles.title: Telegram No. 1078 from Peiping (Completion of Lytton Report and Conference Proposal)
subfiles.to: Henry L. Stimson, Secretary of State

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum reporting the Japanese Cabinet's plan to unify its military, diplomatic, and commercial administrative organs in Manchuria.
subfiles.from: Laurence E. Salisbury, Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Salisbury analyzes a Reuter report that Tokyo will centralize Kwantung Army, government, railway, and consular authority under a military envoy plenipotentiary, expecting General Mutō's appointment and Baron Hayashi heading the Railway.
subfiles.title: Manchuria Situation: Unification of Japanese Administrative Organs in Manchuria

subfiles.about: State Department memorandum summarizing an address by Professor James T. Shotwell on moral disarmament and the changing nature of warfare.
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.summary: Memo summarizes Shotwell's 1933 address arguing disarmament must address chemical/industrial warfare, praising peace-machinery efforts and Germany's reintegration.
subfiles.title: Address on Moral Disarmament by James T. Shotwell
